10755-the-broken-road:
A. E. W. Mason, author of The Four Feathers, published The Broken Road in 1907, a novel of British India and the frontier. Its chapters run from the breaking of a road and Linforth's death through a fort, Lahore, the polo-ground, Peshawar, and the claims of Chiltistan on Shere Ali. Luffe, Sybil Linforth, and Mrs. Oliver move through the tale.

Mason writes of duty, loyalty, and empire on the Northwest Frontier, where roads, regiments, and local princes shape men's fates. The story mixes romance with adventure in high places. Readers get a stirring imperial novel, with India itself as a living presence.
119-a-tramp-abroad:
Mark Twain promised a walking tour of Europe and delivered jokes, detours, and tall tales. A Tramp Abroad, first published in 1880, follows Twain and his agent Harris from Hamburg through Heidelberg and the Alps. The pair mostly ride, float, and argue instead of walking.

Chapters mock German student duels, beer halls, castles, and guides with deadpan invention. Jim Baker's tale of a blue jay and the ascent of the Riffelberg stand out. Illustrations from the first edition add to the comedy. The book remains a favorite of Twain's travel humor.
1847-songs-merry-and-sad:
John Charles McNeill, the North Carolina poet who lived from 1874 to 1907, gathers his lyrics in Songs, Merry and Sad, dedicated to Joseph P. Caldwell, the Old Man. The contents run from The Bride and Isabel to Away Down Home and Vale, with poems of love, loss, and the Carolina countryside.

McNeill's verse is musical and plain-spoken, with autumn nights, droning insects, and hungry lambs in distant pastures giving his poems their weather. The collection shows a regional poet at his best, writing about home with affection rather than nostalgia, and it remains a favorite among readers of Southern verse.
20095-journeys-to-bagdad:
Charles S. Brooks published Journeys to Bagdad in 1915, a book of travel essays with a light touch. Bagdad here stands for the far-off places a clerk dreams of from his desk. Brooks counts himself among those stirred by the smell of hemp and tar. That smell, found near a river ship chandlery, sets him dreaming.

His journeys mix real trips with daydreams of ships and strange towns. Humor keeps the longing sweet rather than sad or bitter. Readers get essays for anyone who has craved escape from routine. Brooks shows how a smell or street can launch the mind abroad.
20807-better-dead:
Clarrie rises to leave as her name is called in Better Dead, a tale from 1896. Love shines in her eyes, yet Andrew holds back from opening the door. He is a Scotch graduate, and besides, she might one day be his wife.

That dry, wry tone marks J. M. Barrie's early comic work. Barrie wrote Better Dead as a young man's skit on university and love. Its jokes turn on pride, shyness, and Scots student life. The slight tale hints at the warmth and whimsy that later made Peter Pan beloved, though here the mood stays light and gently mocking throughout.
21769-songs-of-the-road:
Arthur Conan Doyle steps away from Sherlock Holmes in this 1911 book of his own poems, gathered under the title Songs of the Road. The verses fall into three groups: narrative poems and songs, thoughtful verses, and a mixed final bunch. The opening Hymn of Empire, written for the coronation year, blesses England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland in turn. It reaches as far as Australia and the Maori land.

Other poems take up Arab steeds, empire builders, outcasts, and the faith of an aging man. Doyle's verse is plain, hearty, and built for the open air. Readers who know only the detective stories will find a different Doyle here: a patriot poet singing the road, the sea, and the wide empire.
22382-the-iliad:
The Iliad, Homer's epic of the Trojan War, appears here with explanatory notes. The notes open by summing up the quarrel that drives the poem. Agamemnon must restore the daughter of Chryses, whom he seized.

In revenge, Agamemnon takes Briseis from Achilles instead. Achilles gives her up but refuses to fight for the Greeks. At his request, his mother Thetis petitions Zeus for honor. Zeus grants it, despite Juno's opposition, at Greek expense. That grudge shapes ten years of war in one act. Readers get the classic text with help at hand. The notes guide newcomers through names, gods, and grievances.
22579-bread-overhead:
Bread Overhead is a science fiction story about a future of giant automated bakeries. The catalog record names no author or year. Its comic machinery includes huge serpent-shaped ovens that turn out loaves sealed in clear plastic, each stamped with the Puffyloaf brand mark of two cherubs circling a floating loaf.

Pickup machines gather the loaves at the oven's rear platform, snatching at them like hungry piglets with clean metal claws. The tone is playful satire aimed at mass production and brand worship. Short and brisk, the story suits readers who enjoy mid-century guesses about automation. It also shows how science fiction of that era turned everyday goods into symbols of a push-button future.
22598-the-story-of-the-first-trans-conti:
W. F. Bailey wrote The Story of the First Trans-Continental Railroad, published in 1906. Bailey recounts how the dream of a rail line from the Midwest to the Pacific grew from memorials in Congress into iron fact. The catalog of government publications alone, he notes, lists a great many reports on Pacific railroads.

The sample reaches back to a memorial by Hartwell Carver urging a rail link from Lake Michigan to the Pacific Coast. From such proposals came the Union Pacific and the golden spike era. Bailey writes as a booster-historian, close to the companies and proud of the achievement. His book preserves the promoters' own view of the road that bound a continent together.
2283-the-lost-road:
Richard Harding Davis gathers stories of adventure and war reporting in The Lost Road, a volume spanning soldiers, scouts, and wanderers. The title story leads a set that moves from the tropics to France, with Davis's crisp journalism shaping every scene. His heroes are brave, his villains plain, and his action never stalls.

An introduction by John T. McCutcheon recalls Davis in Vera Cruz, Brussels, and Salonika, adding a memoir flavor to the book. The collection captures the dashing reporter-novelist at his peak. Readers of old-fashioned adventure will find it brisk and colorful.
2392-further-adventures-of-lad:
Albert Payson Terhune returns to his beloved collie Lad in Further Adventures of Lad, a set of stories about the dog's courage, loyalty, and cleverness at Sunnybank. Lad defends his home, rescues children, and outwits thieves, with Terhune's warm narration treating the dog as a full character. The stories blend fact and fiction about a real dog.

Terhune's collie books made him famous and shaped generations of dog lovers. The tales are sentimental but sincere, and Lad's heroics never feel forced. Dog lovers will find a classic to share. Terhune's Sunnybank kennels still exist today as a public park in New Jersey.
2948-where-angels-fear-to-tread:
E. M. Forster's first novel, Where Angels Fear to Tread, begins at Charing Cross, where the Herriton family sees Lilia off to Italy. Philip, Harriet, Irma, and Mrs. Herriton gather with Mrs. Theobald and Mr. Kingcroft, while Miss Abbott arrives with her own relatives. Lilia laughs at the crowd, calls it an ovation, and demands foot-warmers for her first-class carriage.

In Italy Lilia marries rashly, and the Herritons' attempts to rescue her, and later her child, expose English snobbery against Italian feeling. A wife crying while she writes a short letter begging to be saved gives the novel its emotional center. Forster's comedy of manners turns tragic, and the book still reads as a fresh attack on respectability.
3059-the-iliad:
Homer's Iliad appears here in English prose by Andrew Lang, Walter Leaf, and Ernest Myers, in the revised Macmillan edition of 1911. Lang of Merton College, Leaf of Trinity College, and Myers of Wadham College divided the translation, as the prefatory note explains, giving the epic a clear, readable prose form. All twenty-four books run from the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon to the burial of Hector.

A night scene compares Trojan watchfires to stars on a windless night, when peaks, headlands, and glades stand clear and a shepherd's heart is glad. A thousand fires burn on the plain, fifty men by each in blazing gleam. The translation remains a respected prose Iliad, faithful to Homer's story while letting English readers follow the war without verse.
316-the-golden-road:
L. M. Montgomery follows the Story Girl and her Prince Edward Island friends down the golden road of childhood, a highway through the land of lost delight. The book is dedicated to Aunt Mary Lawson, who told many of the tales retold here. Montgomery wrote The Golden Road in 1913, as a sequel to The Story Girl.

Shadow and sunshine mingle as the children tell stories, dream, and watch the years wait beyond. Montgomery writes with warmth and nostalgia, and the novel pairs with The Story Girl as a portrait of a vanished youth. The Story Girl herself, a gifted teller of tales, gives the book its centre and its charm.
3176-the-innocents-abroad:
Mark Twain's 1869 travel book follows a party of American innocents abroad on a grand excursion. Popular talk of the trip, its programme, and its tickets open the account, with the defection of the celebrities who had promised to come. Grand preparations, an imposing dignitary, and the European exodus follow, until the clans assemble and the ship is at sea at last.

From stateroom number ten the pilgrims proceed to average their fellow passengers, endure tribulation among the patriarchs, and seek amusement under difficulties. Twain's humor works by collision: American expectation against European fact, at every port. The book made his name, and it remains the funniest first tour of Europe in American letters.
4069-the-dawn-of-canadian-history-a-chro:
Stephen Leacock's chronicle of Aboriginal Canada opens before European arrival, when uncounted centuries of Native history left few written records. Very few tribes held even a primitive art of writing, though Aztecs and Toltecs of Mexico preserved rulers and great events in pictures.

Leacock sketches the peoples of the North, their ways of life, and the first meetings with explorers. The book belongs to the Chronicles of Canada series, written for general readers in plain, lively prose. Modern readers should note its dated terms and views, while valuing its clear survey of a deep past.
4322-my-three-days-in-gilead:
Elmer U. Hoenshel wrote this travel narrative of three days in Gilead, the biblical land east of the Jordan. His chapters carry him from waiting at Damascus through Bashan, among Bedouins, to Gerasa, up into the mountains, by a watch-tower, and down to the Jordan and its bridge.

Hoenshel writes as a pilgrim and observer, noting the people, camps, and ruins he meets on the road. The book joins scripture geography with firsthand travel, and it suits readers who want a short, vivid account of a Holy Land route. Its charm lies in the pace: three days, closely watched, in an ancient landscape.
4380-under-fire-the-story-of-a-squad:
Henri Barbusse wrote this novel of the First World War from his service in a French infantry squad, translated by Fitzwater Wray. He dedicated it to comrades who fell beside him at Crouy and on Hill 119, in January, May, and September 1915. The contents run from the vision and in the earth to sanctuary, habits, leave, and bombardment.

The squad's life unfolds in trenches, billets, and fatigues, with chapters on the dog, the doorway, big words, and burdens. Barbusse writes without heroics, letting mud, fear, and comradeship speak. Under Fire won the Prix Goncourt, and it remains one of the great novels of the trenches, plain in style and unsparing in truth.
5720-a-shropshire-lad:
Housman's Shropshire Lad gathers short lyrics of youth, love, loss, and the English countryside, introduced in this edition by William Stanley Braithwaite in 1919. The introduction praises how the poems wear the attire of reality in the simplest speech, yet rise into sheer loveliness of spirit. Shropshire hills, lanes, soldiers, and seasons give the poems their setting, while parting and death give them their ache.

Readers meet plain diction carrying deep feeling, with soldiers marching, lovers parting, and young men facing a short life. The poems are brief enough to read one at a time, and they repay slow reading aloud. Housman's collection remains a favorite for those who love English lyric poetry that says hard truths in clear, musical lines.
6103-tales-of-the-road:
Charles N. Crewdson dedicates Tales of the Road to Alex C. Ritchey, salesman and friend, and opens with the claim that the salesman is the steam, and a big part of the engine too, that makes business move. His contents promise the square deal, clerks, cranks and touches, and social arts as salesmen's assets.

Tricks of the trade, the helping hand, first experiences, tactics in selling, cutting prices, canceled orders, and credit men follow. Winning the customer's good will, salesmen's don'ts, merchants met on the road, and hearts behind the order book close the book. Crewdson writes selling as craft and character.
6132-a-man-of-samples-something-about-th:
Wm. H. Maher opens A Man of Samples with a midnight departure: when do you start, Tom, at midnight, good-by, sock it to them, send fat orders. The traveling man is off on a wedding tour, and the narrator, a stock clerk and house salesman for three years, has agreed to take his place for one trip.

As the hour nears, his courage sinks, and he heartily wishes he had never consented. Success on the road gains him nothing, since he means not to continue there, while failure might make his house place less secure. Maher turns one reluctant trip into portraits of men met on the road, with humor and worry.
6150-the-iliad:
Homer's Iliad appears here rendered into English blank verse by Edward, Earl of Derby, in twenty-four books. The preface recalls that in spring 1862, at friends' request, Derby printed for private circulation a small volume of translations, including the first book of the Iliad.

Competent judges praised his attempt to infuse into an almost literal version something of the spirit and simplicity of the great original, encouraging him to continue. The work gave him unfailing and growing interest in intervals of more urgent business, and he finished it with regret. Derby's Iliad prizes fidelity with poetic ease.
642-the-altar-of-the-dead:
Henry James writes of grief and memory in this short novel, published in 1916 in Martin Secker's edition. George Stransom dislikes lean anniversaries, yet keeps one rite each year. It marks the death of Mary Antrim, the girl who was to have been his bride and died of fever before the wedding. No priest and no altar made him widowed; loss alone did.

James writes with quiet, measured prose, following Stransom's private altar of the dead through years of remembrance. The tale asks whom we honor and whom we forgive. It endures as a tender study of mourning, where one man's faithfulness outlasts every other love.
6970-the-history-of-a-mouthful-of-bread:
Jean Mace traces a mouthful of bread through the body, showing its effect on the organization of men and animals. Translated from the eighth French edition by Missus Alfred Gatty, the little work had been adopted by the University Commission at Paris among their prize books. Gatty admits she sat down with no special love for the subject as fare for young people, yet became a thorough convert to the author's way of teaching it.

She argues such a study, pursued as Mace pursues it, proves most useful and most desirable for the young. The book follows food from mouth to muscle and mind, turning digestion into a clear story. It aims to make physiology lively, plain, and memorable for school readers.
6987-five-little-peppers-abroad:
Margaret Sidney continues the Pepper family in Five Little Peppers Abroad, answering friends who begged for more of their good times. Readers had asked for the stories Polly told to keep the children happy in the hard days of the little brown house. They also wanted a book of plays and exploits that could not fit the main history. Parents joined the young in urging a volume that would show the influences shaping the children's lives.

Sidney complied, giving a detailed account meant to throw stronger light on family life in that home. The book gathers tales and games from the Peppers abroad, with illustrations by Fanny Cory. It is a warm family volume, meant for all who loved the five little Peppers and wished to stay longer with them.
7132-the-purple-land-being-the-narrative:
W H Hudson tells The Purple Land as the narrative of Richard Lamb's adventures in the Banda Oriental of South America, in a second edition of 1904 illustrated by Keith Henderson. The preface recalls a first issue in 1885, by Sampson Low, in two slim volumes under the longer, enigmatic title The Purple Land That England Lost. A purple land, Hudson notes, may be found in almost any region, and people count gains, not losses.

A few newspaper notices appeared, and one or two serious journals reviewed the book unfavorably under travels and geography, but the public would not buy, and it fell into oblivion. There it might have slept nineteen years or forever, since a book's sleep is apt to be unawakening. The second edition revived a South American romance of love, wandering, and politics.
8078-the-old-homestead:
Mrs Ann S. Stephens, author of Fashion and Famine and many other popular novels, wrote The Old Homestead as a story of New England farm life. Promoted as a superb story of quaint farm life in the vein then popular both in fiction and on the stage. It follows a farm household through the seasons, work, courtship, and family trouble. Stephens was one of America's most prolific storytellers, and her homestead tale aimed at a wide, family audience.

The novel's charm lies in its domestic detail: the house, the fields, and the neighbours who make a farming community. It belongs to the local-colour tradition that celebrated rural New England before the cities drew its young people away. For readers of old American popular fiction, it is a warm, old-fashioned family story.
91-tom-sawyer-abroad:
Tom Sawyer, fresh from river adventures, itches for a wilder trip. Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer Abroad sends Tom, Huck, and Jim aloft in a balloon built by a mad inventor. The craft drifts over the Atlantic toward Africa and the Sahara.

Huck narrates in his own voice as the boys debate geography, fleas, and disappearing lakes. A caravan, a sandstorm, and a treasure hill test Tom's theories. Jim stands siege in one comic set piece after another. The short novel sends Twain's boys beyond the Mississippi for good. Twain's balloon tale satirizes armchair geography while keeping the boys' friendship at its center.
960-the-tin-woodman-of-oz-a-faithful-sto:
L. Frank Baum wrote this faithful story of the Tin Woodman's astonishing adventure, undertaken with Woot the Wanderer, the Scarecrow, and Polychrome, the Rainbow's Daughter. The Tin Woodman, once a woodman turned to tin, sets out with his friends on a quest that tests his heart, such as it is.

Baum follows the party through Oz lands, with humour, magic, and the Tin Woodman's tender care for all living things. Woot's wonder and Polychrome's grace add colour to the road. The book, dedicated to the son of Baum's son Frank, delights Oz readers as a tale of friendship and a heart that proves itself by deeds.
9748-the-old-gray-homestead:
Frances Parkinson Keyes wrote The Old Gray Homestead in 1919, a quiet story of a farm and its folk. Keyes dedicated the book to farmers and their mothers, wives, and daughters, her neighbors and friends of fifteen years. Sally Gray, plain and plump, opens the tale, trading April talk of heat and mud with her brother Austin. The old gray house and its fields anchor the story.

Chapters follow farm work, family talk, and the slow changes of country life, with warmth and exact detail. Keyes writes with love for rural folk, not condescension. A reader gets a gentle farm novel of the postwar years, full of home feeling and the dignity of farm labor.
9865-java-head:
Joseph Hergesheimer's novel takes its name from a Salem shipping house trading with the East, and it opens with young Laurel Ammidon, just turned twelve, weighing the chairs of her childhood home. The Ammidons are a merchant family whose ships and fortunes reach to Java and China.

As Laurel grows, the family's eastern trade brings home people, goods, and ideas that unsettle old Salem ways. Hergesheimer writes in a rich, careful style, attentive to houses, ships, and manners. The novel gives readers a layered portrait of an American port family facing a changing world.
a-man-of-samples-something-about-the-men:
A Man of Samples, by William H Maher, puts a reluctant substitute into a traveling salesman's shoes. Maher opens at midnight. Tom, the regular road man, is off on a wedding tour. The narrator has agreed to take his trip. He is a stock clerk and house salesman of three years. As the hour comes, his courage sinks in proportion.

He tells himself there is nothing to gain. He will not stay on the road. Failure might make his secure place in the house less safe. He eats a heavy hearted supper, bids his landlady and her daughters a solemn goodbye, and goes to the theater to forget. Chapters follow with the road as it was. Hotels, drummers, and orders fat and thin fill them. A sample case introduces him to men across the Midwest.
a-shropshire-lad:
A Shropshire Lad, by A E Housman, collects the short lyrics that made Housman's name, presented here in a 1919 edition with an introduction by William Stanley Braithwaite. Braithwaite praises the poems for wearing reality plainly while turning, in the simplest speech, to sheer loveliness. One English county supplies the ground: cool, tranquil farmland against which brief lives play out.

The lads of the poems soldier, farm, hang, and die young, and the voice speaking for them mixes irony with tenderness. Housman sets happy and painful images side by side without flinching, a habit his introducer calls Grecian in temper. The poems are brief, rhymed, and built to be remembered, which is why lines from them passed into common speech. Readers meet rural England here at its most beautiful and its most fatalistic at once.
a-tramp-abroad:
Mark Twain's travel book recounts a walking tour through Germany and the Alps, and its text notes it was first published in 1880. Twain travels with a companion and reports, in his mock-serious manner, on hotels, porters, river scenery, and the ordeal of learning German. The contents of this first part run from Hamburg and Frankfurt to Heidelberg and its castle.

Set pieces include the legend of the Knave of Bergen, the strange habits of German university students, and their formal duels, described in fascinated detail. Twain also retells Jim Baker's story of blue-jay language, one of his famous tall tales. The humor rests on an American innocent measuring old Europe and finding both wanting and wonderful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-woodh:
Abraham Woodhead was a voluminous controversial writer born at Almonbury, Yorkshire, about March 1609. He died at Hoxton, Middlesex, on 4 May 1678. Educated at University College, Oxford, he entered in 1624, fellow from 1633 and proctor from 1641. He began, while travelling abroad in 1645, thinking of joining the Catholic Church. Ejected from his fellowship in 1648, he tutored the young Duke of Buckingham and lived with friends until 1654.

In 1654 he and other Catholics bought a house at Hoxton for a community life of devotion and study. Restored to his fellowship in 1660, he soon returned to Hoxton, where he lived on its income until his death, busy with literary labour. His chief works were Ancient Church Government, Guide in Controversies, and four works against Stillingfleet. He also translated St. Teresa's life and St. Augustine's Confessions, and his manuscripts passed to Sir Thomas Brooke's collection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allahabad:
Allahabad is a diocese suffragan to Agra in India, between 28 and 30 degrees north and 77 and 88 degrees east. It covers 150,000 square miles. It sits between Calcutta and Agra east and west, and between Bettiah, the Himalayas, and Nagpur north and south. The mission dates from 1669. Matheus de Castro, a Goan Indian and a Brahmin by caste, was charged by Propaganda with the kingdom of the Great Mogul.

The field proved too vast and the labourers too few. In 1703 Propaganda erected the Prefecture of Tibet and adjoining countries for the Ancona Capuchins. The diocese counts 8,800 Catholics out of 38,174,000 people, mostly Mussulmans and Hindus. Benares, the sacred Hindu city and centre of their religious activity, sits within the diocese. The mission counts 22 Capuchins, 3 secular priests, 18 Christian Brothers, and 74 nuns of the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Six orphanages hold about 450 children, and educational establishments teach 1,468 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arad: Arad was a titular see in Palestine, said to match the hill of Tell Arad on the road from Petra to Hebron, named in Numbers 21:1 and Judges 1:16. Its bishops' list is given in Le Quien's Oriens Christianus, with Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography cited as a further source. The entry is a bare gazetteer note, fixing a biblical place to a former bishop's seat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bagdad:
Bagdad was founded on the Tigris by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur in 762 or 764. He named it Medinet es-Selam, City of Salvation, while Bagdad is said to mean Garden of Dat. For five centuries it served as the rich, brilliant capital of the Arabian Empire. Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, entered it in 1262, and it passed to Kara Koyunlu Turks, then to Tamerlane.

Persians took it in 1517 and ruled, save a short break, until Sultan Murad made it Ottoman in 1638. It remains the chief town of its vilayet, and the most important city of Asiatic Turkey after Damascus and Smyrna. It exports textiles, gold and silverware, horses, and dates, and holds many beautiful mosques and old wall ruins. Its climate is hot, fevers are frequent, and plague sometimes appears, while its population figures are shaky at best.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-csanad:
A diocesan entry covers Csanad, a Hungarian see suffragan to Kalocsa, spanning 13,713 square miles with over two million people, of whom 824,000 were Catholics. It lists a cathedral chapter, 236 parish churches, 1,099 filial churches, and hundreds of clergy, plus male orders and sisters' convents across the diocese.

One of Hungary's oldest sees, Csanad was founded by King Stephen in 1035, its first bishop the Italian abbot Gerard, tutor to Stephen's son. Mongol invasion in the thirteenth century, Serb immigration in the fourteenth, and later Turkish pressure battered it repeatedly. Its baroque cathedral at Temesvar, built 1736 to 1754, is dedicated to St. George, and a seminary for boys rose under Bishop Bonnaz between 1860 and 1889.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gad:
Gad is one name worn by four figures in the Bible: a patriarch, a tribe, a prophet, and a pagan god of fortune. The patriarch was Jacob's seventh son and first by Zilpah, Leah's maid, born in Mesopotamia. At his birth Leah cried Happily, and the name Gad keeps that cry. Scripture names his seven sons and says no more of him himself.

The tribe of Gad settled east of the Jordan, between Manasseh to the north and Reuben to the south, on land prized for herds. Over 40,000 strong in the desert march, the Gadites crossed to help conquer western Palestine, then held the east bank for centuries as its chief Israelite tribe. Warlike and praised in Moses' blessing, they guarded a frontier whose borders shifted with the ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lead:
Lead is a South Dakota diocese erected 6 August 1902, covering all the state west of the Missouri River, 41,759 square miles, with the bishop's residence at Hot Springs. Its ground came from Nebraska's vicariate apostolic, holding about 6,000 Catholics in 1902, including Sioux reservation Indians.

First bishop John Stariha, vicar-general of St. Paul, was consecrated there on 28 October 1902. Born in Carniola in 1845, he had long pastored St. Francis de Sales in St. Paul. Opening the Rosebud Reservation and new railways drew settlers, parishes, churches, missions, and Indian schools. Ill health made him resign in 1909 and return to Austria, and Pius X ratified Joseph Busch of Excelsior, Minnesota, as bishop on 11 April 1910. By 1909 the diocese counted 11,000 white and 6,500 Indian Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-us:
Bread in the liturgy is chiefly the bread of the Eucharist, consecrated at the altar as Christ consecrated bread at the Last Supper. Whether Christ used leavened or unleavened bread is still debated, since John's Gospel and the other Gospels point different ways, and early practice likely used whatever bread lay at hand.

Customs hardened by region: Eastern churches mostly kept leavened bread, while Western churches chose unleavened. The gap fed sharp dispute at the schism, though either kind counts as valid matter. Early faithful brought their own bread and wine to the altar, a custom echoed when a new bishop offers two loaves, one gilded and one silvered, at his consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-aikenhea:
Mary Aikenhead was foundress of the Irish Sisters of Charity, born at Cork in 1787 and dead at Dublin in 1858. 

Accustomed to active charity and feeling called to religious life, she found no order for outside charitable work. Archbishop Murray chose her against her will to found Ireland's Sisters of Charity. She made a three-year novitiate from 1812 to 1815 at York's Micklegate Bar convent, taking the name Sister Mary Augustine, though the world knew her as Mrs Aikenhead. On 1 September 1815 the first members vowed, with her as superior-general. Sixteen years of organising spread the work through hospitals and rescue work. Shattered health made her an invalid in 1831, yet she directed sisters through the 1832 plague, opened new houses, and sent missions to France and Australia, leaving ten institutions flourishing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monad:
Monad means an ultimate, indivisible unit. This entry follows the word from Greek philosophy through Leibniz, for whom it became the keystone of his system. Pythagoras used it for the unity behind all number. Plato's dialogues used its plural for the Ideas. Aristotle treated it as the principle of number itself, without size and unchanging.

Later thinkers stretched it further. Neoplatonists called God the Monad of Monads. Bruno used it for the tiny substances making up reality. Leibniz built his whole account of substance on it. Each monad mirrors the universe with more or less clarity, from bare attraction in minerals up to intellect in the human soul. God harmonised them all in advance, so no monad truly acts on another.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-office-of-the:
The Office of the Dead, in the Roman liturgy, joins First Vespers, Mass, Matins, and Lauds into one long vigil for the departed. Its Vespers sing psalms 114, 119, 120, 129, and 137 with the Magnificat, its Matins hold three nocturns of psalms and lessons, and Lauds close with the Benedictus.

Unlike other offices it lacks Little Hours, Second Vespers, and Compline, and drops introductions, hymns, and doxologies, recalling ancient vigils that ran from evening through night to dawn. Psalms were chosen for verses that speak of death, and the entry explains each part. The psalms were picked for verses that hint at the state of the dead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayers-for-t:
Catholic teaching on prayer for the dead is bound to purgatory and to the communion of saints, an article of the Apostles' Creed. Trent's twenty fifth session defined that purgatory is real, and that souls held there are aided by the suffrages of the faithful, above all by the worthy sacrifice of the altar. That line but sums old teaching.

There the truly penitent who die in God's love ere they have paid by worthy fruits of penance for sins done and left undone are cleansed by purgatorial pains after death. The living ease them by Masses, prayers, alms, and other pious offices. Objectors cite Ecclesiastes on the fallen tree lying where it falls. The line likely but pictures the iron rule of nature in this seen world. Even read of the soul's fate, it says at most that heaven or hell is fixed at death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fothad:
Fothad of the Canon, monk of Fahan-Mura, won Irish clergy lasting freedom from military service with a rhymed legal plea. Bard, counsellor, and tutor to Aedh Oirnidh, high king from 794 to 818, he accompanied the king's expedition against Leinster in 804 and obtained exemption of clergy forever from soldiering. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places him at the close of the eighth century.

His gifts stood so high that Aengus submitted his Felire for Fothad's approval. In return Fothad gave Aengus his Remonstrance to King Aedh, protesting conscription of churchmen. That rhymed judicial opinion, known as a canon or decree, gave him his surname na Canoine. It opens: The Church of the living God let her alone, waste her not. The entry preserves a poet whose verse changed law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-willehad:
Willehad, bishop of Bremen, evangelised Frisia and Saxony between the Weser and the Elbe. Born in Northumberland before 745, friend of Alcuin and probably schooled at York under Egbert, he was sent to Frisia between 765 and 774 with King Alchred's leave. He cannot have been Boniface's disciple, as Baronius claims, since Boniface left England in 718 and died in 754.

At Dockum, where Boniface was martyred, he made many converts. He crossed the Lauwers with little success at Hugmarke, then worked at Drenthe. In 780 Charlemagne sent him to Wigmodia near the North Sea, where he built many churches. The Saxon rising under Widukind in 782 killed companions and destroyed churches, and Willehad fled to Rome. Returning, he became Bremen's first bishop. He died at Blexen on 8 November 789.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-wh:
Thomas Whitbread, alias Harcourt, was a Jesuit provincial executed at Tyburn in June 1679 as a victim of the Popish Plot scare. Born in Essex in 1618, he studied at St-Omer, joined the Jesuits in 1635. Worked on the English mission for more than thirty years, mostly in the eastern counties, rising to provincial in 1678.

In that office he had refused to admit Titus Oates to the Society, and Oates soon fabricated his plot. Whitbread was arrested in London on Michaelmas Day 1678, though illness kept him from Newgate for three months. A first indictment collapsed, but a second trial convicted him with four fellow Jesuits on the perjured testimony of Oates, Bedloe, and Dugdale. He also wrote a devotional work and two short poems.
david-s-little-lad: David's Little Lad, by L, t, meade, the boy's tale. This book preserves that children's story. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
doe-osti-17171710-a-first-look-at-backgr: Silicon detectors for the Electron-Ion Collider got their background check, and this DOE report takes a first look. The pages detail the noise study. The physicists get their baseline. The look was first. The baseline was noise. The study was noise.
doe-osti-2589492-solar-panel-anti-soilin: Solar panels got their anti-soiling test, and this CRADA final evaluates the coatings. The pages record the outcomes. The solar folks get their closeout. The test was anti-soiling. The evaluation was panel. The folks were solar. The coatings were evaluated.
doe-osti-2997455-baseband-digital-networ: LLRF controllers got their analyzer upgrade, and this DOE report covers the baseband digital upgrade. The pages detail the network analyzer work. The RF engineers get their tool. The upgrade was baseband digital. The controllers were LLRF. The engineers got tools.
doe-osti-3000483-assessment-of-benefits-: Solid-state manufacturing got its nuclear benefits, and this DOE assessment covers advanced processes. The pages detail the findings. The reactor builders get their numbers. The processes were solid-state. The numbers were builder. The builders got numbers. The findings were detailed.
doe-osti-3015358-epcape-stratiform-cloud: Cloud scientist Dan Lubin reports on a field campaign that measured how flat, layered clouds — the gray sheets that cover whole regions — reflect and trap heat. Teams gathered data on the clouds' makeup and how they interact with sunlight. The findings help improve the climate models scientists rely on to predict warming and weather patterns.
doe-osti-3018128-cost-competitive-proces: Aged LIBs got oxide-prepared, and this DOE text makes battery-grade competitively. The pages detail the cost findings. The battery folks get their data. The oxides were battery grade. The data were battery. The LIBs were aged. The preparation was oxides.
doe-osti-3022674-high-intensity-gamma-ra: HIγS got radiographically experimented, and this DOE text sources high-intensity gammas. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The source was high intensity. The data were physicist. The gammas were high. The experiments were radiographic.
doe-osti-3024716-resstock-measure-docume: ResStock got HVAC-documented, and this DOE measure covers load flexibility. The pages detail the findings. The building folks get their data. The flexibility was load. The data were building. The HVAC were measure. The flexibility were load. The ResStock were documentation.
doe-osti-3179919-deformation-of-nano-met: Tiny metal glass bent and squished at the nanoscale got its DOE deformation test, and this text makes the nano-glass. The pages detail the results. The materials folks get their data. The test was synthesis. The nanoscale were test.
doe-osti-3364477-a-framework-for-streaml: Data centers and factories are asking the grid for huge amounts of power, and connecting them is slow and messy. This report assesses how utilities currently handle big new loads and sketches fairer, faster ways to do it. The framework aims to keep the lights on without making everyone else pay the price.
doe-osti-3375599-final-technical-report-: Hadron physics got US-Japan-exchanged, and this DOE final covers structure QCD. The pages detail the technical findings. The physicists get their closeout. The program was exchange. The closeout was physicist. The QCD were structure. The exchange were program.
doe-osti-3377979-initial-feasibility-ass: Mixing fibers into 3-D printed parts can make them far stronger — if the fibers land right. This report assesses whether fiber integration via advanced manufacturing is feasible and sketches the broader strategy. The verdict shapes where the technology goes next.
five-little-peppers-abroad:
Margaret Sidney's Five Little Peppers Abroad takes the Pepper family over the ocean, after readers begged for more of their good times. Friends of the family had pressed Sidney for the stories Polly told in the little brown house, and for the plays and exploits that the main series could not hold.

This volume answers a further pressure: a book showing the Little Peppers abroad, where their family life, humour and mutual care meet new scenes. Fanny Y. Cory's illustrations accompany the text. Readers who grew up with the Peppers will enjoy travelling with them again, and new readers will find a warm, old-fashioned family story.
further-adventures-of-lad:
Albert Payson Terhune returned to his collie Lad in Further Adventures of Lad, a second book of tales from Sunnybank, his New Jersey homestead. Terhune's foreword reports that the first Lad book won the old dog a million friends, and that seventeen hundred visitors had come to see Lad's grave. Most of these stories first ran, shortened, in the Ladies' Home Journal.

The tales follow Lad guarding the Place against burglars, tracking, stowing away, and facing intruders, with chapter titles like Hero-Stuff and No Trespassing. Terhune insists the incidents are true and the telling clumsy, a pose his readers loved. Anyone who wants the classic American dog story, sentimental, brave, and country-house cozy, will find Lad in fine form here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OurDailyBread_O:
The January 7, 1966 issue of 'The Poultryman' is a trade newspaper for the poultry industry. Its lead story reports a new broiler house built by Allen's Hatchery of Seaford, Delaware. The house held 108,000 birds. Around that story, the issue carries the ordinary traffic of an industry paper: prices, equipment, and farm news.

Trade papers like this one were the trade's memory of itself. A 108,000-bird house was news in 1966 because it marked the scale farming was reaching. The issue survives in assassination files for reasons of filing rather than content. For readers, it is a clean sample of a farm trade weekly at work, chicken economics reported straight.
joseph-conrad:
Hugh Walpole's Joseph Conrad is a short study of the novelist, published at New York in 1916. Walpole dedicates the book to Sir Sidney Colvin, in friendship. Four parts make up the study: Biography, The Novelist, The Poet, and Romance and Realism. A short bibliography and an American bibliography follow, with an index.

That plan shows Walpole's aim: first the seaman's life, then the maker of novels judged as artist. Treating Conrad as a poet sets this study apart from plain life stories. The romance and realism chapter weighs the two strains in Conrad's sea tales and novels of adventure. Written while Conrad still lived, it is an early act of criticism by a younger novelist.
my-three-days-in-gilead: Elmer U. Hoenshel wrote My Three Days in Gilead, a title that points to the biblical land of Gilead. The hosted sample preserves only the Project Gutenberg file header, with no readable book text at all. No title page, preface, or chapter text survives in the sample. For that reason the book's journey, scenes, and claims cannot be described from the hosted evidence, and only its title and author can be stated with confidence.
nasa-tm-19680012262-calculations-of-non-:
James K. Harrison, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, calculates lunar heat glow in this memorandum. He asks how much infrared radiation from the Moon's surface falls on a small flat plate hovering just above it. The plate's height and tilt both vary in the study.

The Moon's surface does not radiate evenly in all directions, and Harrison assumes that non-diffuse behavior. His calculations compare that realistic case with a perfectly diffuse surface. The heat falling on the plate, he finds, can differ significantly between the two. Landers and hovering instruments needed that difference to predict their own heating.
secret-bread:
F. Tennyson Jesse published this novel with George H. Doran in New York in 1917. Jesse had earlier written The Milky Way and Beggars on Horseback. A short line from Proverbs about bread eaten in secret gives the book its name and its theme.

Book One, called Sowing, opens with high adventure in a farmyard, then moves through a mill, a kitchen, and chapel scenes. A boy grows up amid farm work, faith, and strong feeling on the moor. Jesse builds a slow, close study of a young life and the hidden hopes that shape it.
songs-merry-and-sad: John Charles McNeill, an American poet of North Carolina who lived from 1874 to 1907, wrote Songs, Merry and Sad. He gives the book to Joseph P. Caldwell, called the Old Man. The contents open with The Bride, Oh, Ask Me Not, Isabel, and a piece for Jane's birthday. A Secret, The Old Bad Woman, Valentine, and A Photograph follow, and later heads name home songs, an Easter hymn, a Christmas hymn, and When I Go Home.
tales-of-the-road: Charles N. Crewdson wrote Tales of the Road in 1905, with art by J. J. Gould, and gave the book to Alex C. Ritchey, a salesman and his friend. Eighteen parts cover the work of traveling salesmen, from The Square Deal Wins and Tricks of the Trade to Tactics in Selling, Cutting Prices, Canceled Orders, and Hearts Behind the Order Book.
the-adventures-of-old-mr-toad: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Old Mr. Toad, with art by Harrison Cady, in 1920, a Smiling Pool tale in twenty-three chapters. Heads track Jimmy Skunk's puzzle, a hunt for Old Mr. Toad, his music bag and queer tongue, a shadow over the pool, his babies at the pool kindergarten, and a lesson learned at the close.
the-altar-of-the-dead:
Henry James wrote this long story, shown here in a London edition from Martin Secker first issued in 1916 and set from the Definitive Edition text. Its main figure, Stransom, has kept one date sacred for years: the day Mary Antrim died. She was to have been his wife, but a harsh fever took her after the wedding day had been set.

Grief rules Stransom's house and habits long after that loss. He has done much in the world, the opening says, except one thing: he has never forgotten her. Memory acts like a priestless altar in his life, and each year the date takes hold of him anew.
the-broken-road: A. E. W. Mason wrote The Broken Road, dated 1907. Mason had also written Four Feathers, The Truants, and Running Water. The chapters start with The Breaking of the Road and Inside the Fort. Linforth's Death and Luffe Looks Forward come next. A Magazine Article, A Long Walk, and In the Dauphiné lead to A String of Pearls. The Invidious Bar, Shere Ali meeting an old friend, News from Mecca, and Sybil Linforth's Loyalty fill the late list. A Gift Misunderstood is the last head shown.
the-cockaynes-in-paris-or-gone-abroad:
Blanchard Jerrold wrote this comic account of the English abroad, with sketches by Gustave Dore and other pictures drawn from a French point of view. John Camden Hotten published it in London at Piccadilly. A picture caption shows Mi Lord Anglais at Mabille, smiling and splendid, at ease among French dancers.

Jerrold's preface looks back with mixed feelings. The Cockaynes' story was written some years earlier, when Paris stood at her best and brightest, the English quarter was crowded, and the Emperor was at St. Cloud. France then seemed set to become the richest and strongest country in the world. Where the Cockaynes carried guide-books and opera-glasses into raptures, dismal ruins now stand. The Vendome Column is a stump, wreathed with a huge immortelle and capped with the tricolor.
the-copyright-question-a-letter-to-the-t:
George N. Morang of Toronto published The Copyright Question in 1902 as a letter to the secretary of the Toronto Board of Trade, dated February 19 of that year. The board's council had backed a plan drawn from a bill proposed in 1895 by Mr. Hall Caine.

Under that plan, a book would have to be printed and bound in Canada to gain Canadian copyright, and stay in Canadian print to keep it. If a book were not printed in Canada within a fair time, the government could license a Canadian publisher to print it, with safeguards giving the owner a fair royalty. Morang traces the plan to talks in 1895 between Caine, speaking for English authors, Mr. Daldy for English publishers, and Canadian publishers, papermakers, printers, and bookbinders.
the-dawn-of-canadian-history-a-chronicle:
Stephen Leacock wrote The Dawn of Canadian History as part of the Chronicles of Canada, a set in thirty-two volumes edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, printed at Toronto in 1915. His contents run from Before the Dawn and Man in America through the aborigines of Canada, the legend of the Norsemen, and the Bristol voyages, closing with a note on sources.

Chapter I grants that Canada is a new country in one sense: European settlement there goes back only three hundred years. Its written history is a little span beside the long annals of Europe and the East. In another sense, he argues, part of it may be the oldest country in the world. The planet itself began, on the nebular theory, as a fiery molten mass cooling into the globe we know.
the-golden-road:
L. M. Montgomery wrote The Golden Road. She dedicates the book to the memory of Aunt Mary Lawson. Aunt Mary told her many of the tales the Story Girl repeats. A foreword looks back at youth as a road. The road runs through the Land of Lost Delight. Shadow and sunshine were sweetly mixed there.

Chapter I is called A New Departure. It opens on a wild November night. The young folk sit in a half-circle round a wood fire. The fire burns in Uncle Alec's kitchen. The narrator says he has thought of something amusing for the winter. The foreword frames the tales to come. They are a keepsake of the golden road of youth. Those memories, Montgomery says, are among the dearest things a person owns.
the-history-of-a-mouthful-of-bread:
Jean Mace wrote The History of a Mouthful of Bread, on the effect of food on the organization of men and animals. The book was translated from the eighth French edition by Mrs. Alfred Gatty. Extracts from the preface to the English edition note that the University Commission at Paris adopted the volume among its prize books.

Gatty admits she began with doubt that the subject suited young people, then became a firm convert to the author's views. The book speaks in letters to a child, at first to a little girl. Difficult facts of science are set out with quaint, droll comparisons meant to win smiles while the lesson lands.
the-iliad: Homer's Iliad appears here in English prose, done by Andrew Lang, Walter Leaf, and Ernest Meyers, fellows respectively of Merton College, Oxford, Trinity College, Cambridge, and Wadham College, Oxford. Macmillan published this revised edition in London in 1911. Only the title page and the contents are present here, so the translation itself does not appear. The contents run from a prefatory note through the books of the poem in sequence, laying out the whole architecture of the epic of Achilles and the Trojan War in bare headings.
the-innocents-abroad: Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad is drawn here from the 1869 first edition. Only the contents are present in this record. The travel narrative itself does not appear. The chapter summaries read like jokes in miniature. The excursion's programme opens them. The celebrities defect at once. Horse-billiards and a synagogue enliven the sea days. Mr. Blucher gives his opinions. A fossil community waits in the Azores. The Pillars of Hercules follow. A private frolic in Africa closes the list shown. It beards a Moorish garrison without loss of life.
the-jericho-road: W. Bion Adkins wrote this little book for the Odd Fellows. He also wrote Twelve Steps Toward Heaven. The book appeared in 1901. He dedicated it to his worthy and gentle brothers. He hoped it would spur greater effort for the beloved order. An opening comparison sets the theme. Rivers run forever yet are never passed. Winds go forever yet are never gone. Odd-Fellowship is like both. Only the dedication and motto pages are present here. The body of the book does not appear.
the-leicestershires-beyond-baghdad: Edward J. Thompson, holder of the Military Cross, wrote a First World War account of his regiment service beyond Baghdad. Only the title page and publication details of the first edition, issued by the Epworth Press in London, are present here. Thompson other books named on the page include Mesopotamian verses and Ennerdale Bridge. The narrative of the Leicestershire regiment march and fighting in Mesopotamia is absent from this record beyond that title page.
the-lost-road:
The Lost Road gathers ten novels and stories by Richard Harding Davis. Among them are The Miracle of Las Palmas, The Men of Zanzibar, The Long Arm, The Buried Treasure of Cobre, and Somewhere in France. An introduction by John T. McCutcheon, titled With Davis in Vera Cruz, Brussels, and Salonika, is part memorial. McCutcheon finds it hard to realize that Davis has covered his last story and will not be seen again among the men who follow the war game.

He calls it bitter irony that Davis was torn away in the middle of the greatest event of all, with the story unfinished. Yet Davis left at the flood tide, McCutcheon writes, still supreme as the best reporter in his country. The collection thus reads as both fiction and tribute to a famous correspondent.
the-old-gray-homestead:
Frances Parkinson Keyes published The Old Gray Homestead in 1919 and dedicated it to the farm families who had been her neighbors for fifteen years. She calls it a quiet story of a farm. The first chapter opens on a hot April day, with Sally Gray driving home from teaching school with her brother Austin.

Austin is lean, dark, and bitter, worn down by farm hardship, while Sally is plain, plump, and calm. She wishes he could find money, love, or some encouragement. Keyes builds the tale on close knowledge of country people, their talk, their mud, their weather, and their hopes.
the-old-homestead:
Mrs. Ann S. Stephens wrote The Old Homestead, a story of New England farm life. Stephens was a prolific novelist, author of Fashion and Famine, The Heiress, and many other tales listed on the title page. A publisher's notice praises her plots, her knowledge of human nature, and her young lovers and their trials.

The first chapter, The Father's Return, opens with a child kneeling by a pauper bed and wondering if he will come. Stephens mixes pathos with home and fireside feeling. The notice promises an absorbing plot and characters true to nature, in the popular vein of farm-life fiction and stage plays of the day.
the-purple-land-being-the-narrative-of-o:
W. H. Hudson tells, through narrator Richard Lamb, of adventures in the Banda Oriental in South America, in a second edition of 1904 illustrated by Keith Henderson. Hudson's preface recalls the first issue of 1885 under the longer title naming the purple land that England lost.

That first edition drew few and mostly unkind notices, was shelved as travel, and soon vanished. Friendly men of letters rescued it, and Hudson revised wording throughout and cut passages for the reprint. Readers get both an adventure narrative and an unusually frank account of an author's first book failing and returning.
the-secret-chamber-at-chad:
Everett Evelyn-Green's The Secret Chamber at Chad opens with a mysterious visitor, according to its contents. Later chapters name the household at Chad and Brother Emmanuel. A travelling preacher, a warning, and a search follow. From peril to safety closes the list of ten chapters.

Chapter one shows the great house wrapped in sleep. June moonlight strikes its gray masonry with strong white light. Castellated turrets and twisted chimneys stand out against a pine wood. Chad had been shorn of glory during the Wars of the Roses, the narrator explains. One of its two quadrangles lay in ruins and was never rebuilt. The seventh Henry now sits on the throne. Bosworth Field ended the strife between York and Lancaster, and the household rejoices in the peace.
the-texan-scouts-a-story-of-the-alamo-an: Joseph A. Altsheler's Texan Scouts, a story of the Alamo and Goliad dated 1913, continues the fortunes of Ned Fulton from The Texan Star, as its own note explains. The pages present here stop at the title and the first contents entries. Those entries open in a storm, move to captives and a fight with Urrea, and arrive at Santa Anna's advance and the Alamo itself. Readers can see the historical ground the novel covers, while Altsheler's battle narrative remains beyond this record.
the-tin-woodman-of-oz-a-faithful-story-o:
L. Frank Baum's Tin Woodman of Oz is dedicated to his grandson Frank Alden Baum and introduced by the author's own letter to readers. Baum says correspondents kept asking what became of the pretty Munchkin girl Nick Chopper meant to wed, before the Wicked Witch's spell on his axe. He wondered himself, he admits, until Woot the Wanderer took up the matter. The Tin Woodman has now found her, after many thrilling adventures.

Baum shares letters showing readers from a boy of five to a married couple past seventy, all eager for Oz. His questioner, a college professor, wanted to know what age his books suit. Baum's answer is the whole audience. The quest that follows, with the Scarecrow and Polychrome helping, settles one of the oldest loose ends in the Oz series.
tom-sawyer-abroad:
Mark Twain lets Huck Finn ask whether Tom Sawyer could stay satisfied after their river adventures and Jim's freeing. Fame only poisoned Tom for more, Huck says. The village gave them a torchlight procession, and boys knuckled to Tom Sawyer the Traveler.

Old Nat Parsons, the postmaster and the village's only rival traveller for thirty years, threatens Tom's glory. Contents promise a balloon ascension, storms, a caravan, a disappearing lake, treasure hill, and a sandstorm across thirteen chapters. Readers get Huck's voice narrating Tom's hunger for adventure, now pointed at Africa by balloon.
under-fire-the-story-of-a-squad: Henri Barbusse's Under Fire, the story of a squad, was translated by Fitzwater Wray. Barbusse dedicates the book to comrades who fell beside him at Crouy and on Hill 119 in 1915. The contents list twenty-four chapters, from The Vision and In the Earth to bombardment, the chapter called Under Fire, and The Dawn. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the squad's story itself does not appear.
unleavened-bread:
Robert Grant published Unleavened Bread with Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1900. The novel stands in three books whose titles chart a life: The Emancipation, The Struggle, and The Success. Chapter one opens as wedding guests leave a country house on a bright September night, driving off in hay carts with songs and laughter floating back down the road.

Among the last to leave are Babcock and Selma White. Selma rides home in a chaise, well wrapped against the autumn air, in no hurry over the seven miles. Festive nights and the open devotion of a city young man are new things in her quiet life, though she has always been treated with care. Grant sets her at a turning point: a woman used to being tacitly placed first in her small world, now facing a wider one.
where-angels-fear-to-tread:
E. M. Forster opens Where Angels Fear to Tread at Charing Cross station in London. A crowd has come to see Lilia Herriton off to Italy. Her brother-in-law Philip, her mother-in-law, and small Irma all crowd the platform. Lilia laughs without pause at the fuss and calls it an ovation fit for royalty.

Philip pours out last advice on where to stop and how to learn Italian. He urges her to leave the track, see small towns like Gubbio and Cortona, and love the Italian people. Italy, he says, is no mere museum of old art. Forster's first novel turns a widow's trip into love, scandal, and clash of English and Italian ways.
willis-the-pilot-a-sequel-to-the-swiss-f:
Willis the Pilot continues the tale of the Swiss Family Robinson, as its preface explains. Lee and Shepard printed the book in Boston in 1875. The preface retells the source story: a Swiss clergyman sailed with his wife and four sons for a Pacific island. A storm drove their ship off course near New Guinea and wrecked it on an unknown coast.

Youth in the present day, the preface says, loves adventure and tales of new lands. That taste keeps the Robinson book popular with old and young alike. The sequel adds a pilot named Willis and new travels for the castaway family. Sea peril, natural history, and tales fill the pages. Castaway adventure drives the book.
